title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design used shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reused the same deterministic validator for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring. These two frozen design choices produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the preregistered primary estimand (paired difference in safe‑deploy rate) effectively untestable for generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. Execution artifacts (N=400 paired tasks; 800 episodes) show baseline_success_count = 400/400 and guarded_success_count = 400/400, observed paired difference = 0.0, preregistered permutation p = 1.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded outcomes, a diagnostic explanation of the ceiling, a compact execution accounting table, a representative task worked example, and artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations to preserve signal for future evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into concrete network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work demonstrates LLMs can synthesize syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings while verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variance, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes? We study this question operationally by preregistering and executing a paired design comparing a verifier‑augmented pipeline (guarded) to an LLM‑only pipeline (baseline) on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark.

Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 paired tasks.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_generation semantics; (2) exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing a deterministic ceiling that renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard dynamics in this execution; (3) a compact worked example and execution accounting; and (4) artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.
sections.related_work: This study connects four threads: intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Intent translation and configuration generation with LLMs have been demonstrated in recent work (e.g., Nguyen Van Tu et al., "Intent‑Based Network Configuration Using Large Language Models", 2024; F. Li et al., "PreConfig", 2024) showing plausible configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds. Verifier‑guided loops and verifier‑guided fine‑tuning in IaC (e.g., Jana et al., "TerraFormer", 2026) report correctness gains in infrastructure provisioning contexts, motivating analogous integrations for NetOps. Deterministic verifiers and reachability analyses are mature tools for detecting configuration errors offline and in emulated environments (e.g., Xinzhe Liu et al., 2025). Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct/style multi‑agent approaches and RAG pipelines) expand functionality in AIOps and RCA tasks but introduce failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, miscalibrated confidence) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments (see Pei et al., "Flow‑of‑Action", 2025; survey evidence on evaluation gaps and trustworthy agentic AI). The cited prior works used in this positioning are archived and verified in the artifact bundle; key records include the intent→configuration and verifier‑guided IaC sources referenced above (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. We preregistered the study as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1. The primary confirmatory estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided, α=0.05). The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; we also report an exact McNemar two‑sided test for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics and the critical shared‑generation choice. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Crucially, preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation that was delivered identically to both the baseline and guarded episodes. This choice intentionally isolated the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs rather than exposing independent generator variance between conditions. Because one generator call served both episodes per pair, model_calls_used = 400 while planned episodes = 800; this mapping is reflected in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts.

Explicit design consequence. We preregistered and executed the configuration above; therefore the methodological fact that shared_initial_generation combined with reuse of the same deterministic validator makes the preregistered primary estimand effectively untestable in this run is intentional and must be stated up front. When a deterministic validator deterministically accepts a shared candidate, both conditions necessarily record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference is forced to zero; the observed null is therefore a design consequence, not a general null statement about verifier utility.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested one shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and—only in the guarded episode—routed it to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation using a deterministic rule set recorded in validator_trace entries. The preregistered repair policy allowed up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before/after, and final validity decisions were logged. In this execution repair_applied = false across episodes.

Task generation, deterministic replay, and exclusion rules. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task record contains structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; reproducible simulator errors or nondeterministic replay would lead to exclusion per the missingness_plan. In this run all three‑replay checks passed and no exclusions were applied (complete_pairs = 400).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded. (See Table 1 captioned with these artifact‑grounded numbers.)

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The primary contingency counts were baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen’s h = 0.0. These numbers are reproduced directly from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/*).

Repair and rollback observations. Across 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. This explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes.

Representative task worked example. A compact representative example illustrates the mechanics: task-000001 (pair-000001) instructs migrating edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600 with a safe shutdown→change→restore sequence. The shared gpt‑5‑mini candidate (stored under execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) matched the reference sequence; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated the candidate (validation_after.valid = true) and no repair was applied. Both baseline and guarded episodes therefore recorded success for this pair—mirroring the n_11 pattern across the full corpus.

Difficulty labels and diversity. Per‑task difficulty labels are recorded in the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl. Representative sample entries (the first six representative tasks included in the artifact bundle) show one medium, two hard, and three very_hard examples, illustrating benchmark pattern diversity at the sample level. The full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 tasks are archived and available to auditors in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; the manuscript reports the representative sample and points auditors to the artifact bundle for full aggregations performed externally to this text.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general.

Consequences for power and inference. The preregistered power calculation assumed within‑pair variability and non‑ceiling baseline rates; both assumptions were violated by the deterministic ceiling, invalidating the original power rationale. Exact p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the observed data but do not adjudicate whether a runtime guard would improve outcomes under an alternative design that preserves generator variance.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark hardening recommendations. Using archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete preregistered mitigations to preserve signal for generator×guard interactions:
(1) independent_condition_generation = true so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has opportunities to accept, block, or request repair; (2) use distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to avoid conflating acceptance and scoring; (3) include controlled adversarial seeding to guarantee nontrivial baseline failure rates for power; (4) perform difficulty‑stratified sampling to ensure sufficient very_hard tasks; (5) instrument and preregister repair and time‑to‑rollback metrics as primary/secondary outcomes. All of these steps are implementable using the existing task generator and validator traces archived in execution/* and analysis/* and will preserve inferential signal in future confirmatory runs.

Operational implications. For practitioners, the experiments underscore two practical lessons: (i) designs that remove generation variance can hide potential benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human review) are important when measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should therefore preserve generator variance or inject controlled perturbations so the guard can demonstrably affect outcomes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline under shared_initial_generation semantics. Under the frozen design (shared generation + single deterministic validator used for both runtime and scoring) every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions yielded 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling is a design outcome that makes the preregistered primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop effects in this execution. The full execution and analysis artifacts are archived and reproduce the numbers above; we provide artifact‑grounded recommendations (independent generation, heterogeneous validators, adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification) to harden future benchmarks so they retain statistical signal for evaluating runtime verification utility. The archived artifacts, validator traces, and task manifests support reproducible follow‑on confirmatory designs that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors under preserved generator variance.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory): Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini. Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints were selected pre‑lock by the Research Director and limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. Permitted tools and capabilities: hosted model API calls, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across episodes). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). Autonomous literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting occurred post‑lock under the master prompt autonomy constraints; no human manually edited the technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for follow‑on preregistered work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript reports representative sample counts to illustrate benchmark diversity but does not invent aggregated counts absent explicit artifact summarization in the manuscript body.
